title: Given a `List<Employee>`, find any employee from the "HR" department, returning an `Optional<Employee>`, and demonstrate handling the empty case with `orElse`, `orElseGet`, and `orElseThrow`. Explain the difference between `orElse` and `orElseGet`.
shortTitle: Find any employee from HR using Optional
keyPoints: filter(e -> e.getDepartment().equals("HR")).findAny() returns an Optional<Employee> that is empty when no HR employee exists
orElse(value) always evaluates its argument, even when the Optional has a value, so avoid it when the fallback is expensive
orElseGet(supplier) only runs the supplier when the Optional is empty, making it the lazy and preferred fallback
orElseThrow() throws NoSuchElementException, while orElseThrow(supplier) lets you throw a domain exception you choose
findAny() may return any matching element and is faster on parallel streams, while findFirst() is deterministic
Never call Optional.get() without checking isPresent() first, as it throws NoSuchElementException on an empty Optional
Optional is designed as a return type for possibly-absent results, not as a field type or method parameter

s1_definition.oneliner: Use stream filter plus findAny to get an Optional<Employee>, then unwrap it with orElse for an eager default, orElseGet for a lazy default, or orElseThrow when absence is an error.
s1_definition.profdef:
Optional is a container that holds either one value or nothing, forcing the caller to handle the empty case.

- **Optional<T>** – a box that is either present with a value or empty, replacing a raw `null` return.
- **filter(predicate).findAny()** – keeps only matching employees and returns the first one it finds as an `Optional<Employee>`.
- **orElse(fallback)** – returns the value if present, otherwise the fallback, but the fallback expression is always evaluated.
- **orElseGet(supplier)** – returns the value if present, otherwise calls the supplier, which runs only when the Optional is empty.
- **orElseThrow(supplier)** – returns the value if present, otherwise throws the exception you build in the supplier.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Priya asks the teller for any available HR officer to approve her form. The teller checks the duty roster, which is like an Optional: it either names an officer or it is blank. If an officer is on duty, the teller calls that person (the value is present). If the roster is blank, orElse would be like always phoning the backup office even when an officer was free, wasting the call, while orElseGet only phones the backup when the roster is truly empty. orElseThrow is the teller refusing to proceed and raising a formal complaint when no officer exists at all.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  List<Employee>
       │
       │  stream()
       ▼
  Stream<Employee>
       │
       │  filter(e -> e.getDepartment().equals("HR"))
       ▼
  Stream<Employee>  (only HR)
       │
       │  findAny()
       ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │      Optional<Employee>        │
  │                                │
  │   present ?                    │
  └───────────────────────────────┘
       │                     │
   present                 empty
       │                     │
       ▼                     ▼
  return value       pick a fallback path
                           │
        ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
        ▼                  ▼                  ▼
  orElse(value)     orElseGet(supplier)  orElseThrow(supplier)
  (eager default)   (lazy default)       (raise exception)
```

```text
  orElse vs orElseGet when value IS present

  opt = Optional.of("Priya")

  opt.orElse( build() )        opt.orElseGet( () -> build() )
        │                              │
        ▼                              ▼
   build() RUNS                  build() SKIPPED
   (wasted work)                 (lazy, efficient)
        │                              │
        ▼                              ▼
   returns "Priya"                returns "Priya"
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
At the National Bank of India, Rajesh needs to find any HR officer from a list of staff. The officer might not be on the list, so instead of returning a raw value that could be null, the search returns an `Optional<Employee>`. That box either holds an officer or is empty, and it forces Rajesh to decide what happens when nobody is found.

When the box holds a value, all three unwrapping methods return it. The difference shows up only when the box is empty. `orElse` hands back a value you prepared in advance, but it prepares that value every time, even when the box was full, so it wastes work if the fallback is expensive. `orElseGet` takes a supplier and runs it only when the box is empty, which is why it is the better choice whenever building the default costs anything.

When absence is not a normal outcome but a real error, `orElseThrow` stops the flow and raises an exception. The no-argument form throws `NoSuchElementException`, and the supplier form lets Rajesh throw a domain exception that the rest of the banking system understands.

The mistakes to avoid are calling `get()` without checking, returning `null` instead of `Optional.empty()`, and reaching for Optional as a field or parameter. Used as a return type for a lookup that may find nothing, Optional makes the empty case impossible to ignore.

Remember one sentence: filter then findAny gives you an Optional, orElse evaluates its default eagerly while orElseGet evaluates lazily, and orElseThrow turns an empty result into a clear error.
